title: Going deeper
lede: Five more questions — about the ground under your plan rather than the plan itself: what it rests on, who was heard, what was set aside, and who holds it together. Two minutes; the written version follows by email like the first.

questions.text: Some of what your strategic plan rests on you know, and some you believe. Could you point to which is which?
answers: Yes — the facts have sources, the assumptions are written down, and someone's checking them.
We know the difference in our heads; it isn't written down.
We treat it all as known.
We haven't asked ourselves that.

questions.text: Who was asked what they needed before the direction was set — and who was on the list and never heard from?
answers: We can name who was asked, how many answered, and who we missed.
We asked widely; we couldn't tell you the response rate.
Leadership and the board.
Mostly the people who set it.

questions.text: What did you decide not to do — and could leadership explain why to the board, or to anyone who asked?
answers: Yes — the paths we didn't take, and why, are written down and were shared.
We weighed options; the recommendation is what got shared.
There was one obvious path, so we took it.
We haven't ruled anything out — which may be the problem.

questions.text: When did one of your leaders last have a real conversation with a member or customer they didn't already know personally?
answers: This quarter — it's a habit with a name.
This year, informally.
We have survey numbers.
We know our members; we haven't felt the need.

questions.text: If the one person who holds a key process together left this month, what happens?
answers: We've named who those people are, and there's a plan for each.
We know who they are; nothing's written down.
We'd manage — we always have.
I'd rather not think about it.

bands.label: Solid ground
bands.text: The plan stands on things you can point to: facts with sources, assumptions written down, people who were actually asked, paths declined for reasons someone could repeat, and a name against every person who holds a process together. That is the part most plans skip, and it is what carries one through a change of leadership. What we'd look at with you is whichever of the five is thinnest — there is always one.

bands.label: Partly assumed
bands.text: Some of what the plan rests on is known and some is believed, and the difference lives mostly in people's heads. That is normal, and it isn't a weakness until an assumption gets treated as a fact and nobody checks it again. The fix is small: write down which is which, name who wasn't heard from, and say out loud what was set aside and why. An afternoon, usually — and it changes how the next board conversation goes.

bands.label: Unexamined
bands.text: The plan may well be right, but the ground under it hasn't been looked at: what it rests on is treated as known, the people it affects were mostly the people who wrote it, nothing was ruled out, and the person holding a key process together has no name on paper. None of that shows until something moves — a leader leaves, a member leaves, an assumption turns out wrong. We'd start there, before touching the plan itself: a short pass over these five things, with your board in the room.
